How do characteristic elements of public spaces affect spatial vitality? An analysis of inﬂuence effects and response thresholds from the Hangzhou section of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal

Wei Dai ●Peilun Zhu ●Xihui Wang ●Xinyi Huang ●Jiayang Jia ●Ran Kang

Received: 14 August 2025 / Accepted: 27 August 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Spatial vitality is theoretically grounded in classic urban planning and human settlement theories, including Jane Jacobs’ Urban Diversity, Jan Gehl’s Social Space, and Kevin Lynch’s Image of the City. It is explicitly deﬁned as a public space’s capacity to attract sustained recreational engagement and foster diverse social interaction, and it serves as a core metric for evaluating urban public space quality and human settlements development amid global stockbased urban renewal. This study addresses a well-documented critical gap: while macro- and meso-scale urban vitality research is oversaturated, prevailing analytical models are predominantly limited to linear correlation analysis. These models lack quantitative threshold-based causal inference for nonlinear vitality-generating mechanisms in micro-scale waterfront contexts. This study takes 56 micro-scale waterfront public spaces along the UNESCO World Heritage Hangzhou Section of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal as its research samples. It develops a “built environment-functional activity-spatial vitality” analytical framework, ﬁrst identiﬁes core vitality drivers via correlation analysis, and ﬁnally quantiﬁes nonlinear response thresholds for national Grade I vitality standards through Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and Spatial Lag Model (SLM)-corrected regression that controls for spatial spillover effects. Results reveal locational centrality, public transport station accessibility, water surface ratio, cultural and sports facility density, and functional integration degree as core vitality drivers. These drivers present heterogeneous thresholds across ecological conservation, commercial-business, and residential living functional typologies, a difference that is interpreted as driven by divergent user demands and context-speciﬁc vitality generation pathways. This study advances prevailing linear correlation-focused models by establishing typologyspeciﬁc, quantiﬁable thresholds for vitality enhancement. It explicates the core “built environment optimizationfunctional activity catalysis-sustained vitality generation” mechanism, and further provides empirically grounded, threshold-informed planning guidance and a replicable analytical framework for micro-scale urban public space vitality research.

## Introduction

Public space vitality serves as a core quantitative metric for quantifying the quality of urban public spaces and the quality of human settlement development, the magnitude of which directly reﬂects the utilization efﬁciency, social cohesion, and sustainable development potential of urban spaces (Cai et al., 2025; Zhang et al,2025). Globally, most developed cities have entered the stock-based urban renewal phase. Challenges including morphological homogenization, functional monotonicity, and vitality degradation of public spaces—driven by standardized development practices—have become a bottleneck constraining the high-quality development of urban human settlements (Guo et al., 2022). The traditional urban renewal paradigm, which is predicated on large-scale demolition and physical space retroﬁtting, is no longer adequate to resolve the challenge of public space vitality degradation in the stock-based urban development context. It is therefore critical to elucidate the inherent causal mechanisms linking the characteristic elements of public spaces to spatial vitality, so as to establish an empirical basis for the high-quality optimization of urban public spaces. Over the past century, scholarly inquiry into urban public space vitality has undergone extensive proliferation, yielding a sequentially developed theoretical lineage. In 1929, Clarence Perry ﬁrst formalized the Neighborhood Unit concept within a spatial unit-centered analytical framework, establishing the foundational theoretical link between public space layout, residents’ daily social interactions, and neighborhood vitality (Perry, 2015). In 1960, Kevin Lynch put forward the Theory of the Image of the City in his landmark monograph, developing a pioneering analytical framework that links spatial form, psychological cognition, and behavioral decision-making from the perspective of users’ spatial perception (Lynch, 1984). In 1961, Jane Jacobs formalized the Theory of Urban Diversity, positing that spatial vitality is rooted in the diversity of the built environment, and delineating four core determinants shaping urban public life (Jacobs, 1992). In 1971, Jan Gehl proposed the human-centered Theory of Social Space, elucidating the human-centered core of urban vitality and quantifying the causal transmission mechanism through which spatial attributes drive the emergence of spatial vitality (Gehl, 2011). In 1989, Wayne Attoe and Donn Logan formalized the Urban Catalyst Theory, elucidating the causal mechanisms through which tangible and intangible urban attributes drive the generation of spatial vitality, thus extending and complementing the analytical framework ﬁrst established by Jan Gehl (Attoe and Logan, 1989). In 1991, Henri Lefebvre’s monograph The Production of Space was released, introducing his landmark Theory of the Production of Space to academia, which advanced the foundational concept that “the built environment shapes vitality”, ﬁrst proposed by Perry and Jacobs from a critical sociological perspective (Lefebvre, 2012). In 1993, Peter Calthorpe established himself as a foundational theorist of the New Urbanism movement, developing the movement’s theoretical framework rooted in Jane Jacobs’ foundational philosophy of urban diversity, extending the scope of spatial vitality research beyond the paradigm of environment-behavior studies to integrate the holistic framework of urban sustainable development (Calthorpe, 2014). Building on these theoretical frameworks, scholars worldwide have advanced multifaceted research inquiries into public space vitality, organized along four analytical dimensions: theoretical underpinnings, research scales, driving determinants, and enhancement strategies. This body of work has established an interdisciplinary research paradigm (Liu et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Doan and Zhang, 2025). In terms of theoretical underpinning, extant scholarship has drawn on theoretical frameworks spanning urban planning, environment-behavior studies, and urban catalyst, to conduct systematic theoretical explorations of the deﬁnition and core connotations of public space vitality (A et al., 2020; Paudel and Pant, 2023). Speciﬁcally, work in this domain was published in 1998, when Montgomery operationalized the construct of public space vitality, disaggregating its core conceptual connotations into three interlocking dimensions: perceptible place identity, sustained social interaction, and multifaceted functional and cultural attributes. Critically, he posited that the fundamental essence of vitality lies in the dynamic synergistic coupling between a space’s physical form, human behavioral practices, and place-speciﬁc cultural context (Montgomery, 1998). Building on this foundational conceptualization, Zhao and Wang (2012) systematically unpacked the dual nature of public space vitality: endogenous place vitality deﬁned as a space’s inherent capacity to sustainably attract public participation and foster diverse social interactions, and exogenous vitality spillover effects whereby the space acts as an urban catalyst to drive functional renewal,

Extending this line of inquiry into critical sociological theory, Mouratidis and Poortinga (2020) advanced the foundational proposition that the core essence of public space vitality resides in the organic integration of a space’s materiality, sociality, and subjectivity. This landmark contribution signiﬁcantly expanded the sociological scope of academic conceptualizations of public space vitality (Mouratidis and Poortinga, 2020). Most recently, building on these prior conceptual advancements, Osunkoya and Partanen (2024) conceptualized public space vitality as a space’s inherent capacity to accommodate and catalyze diverse outdoor activities by grounding their work in the environment-behavior studies paradigm and the tripartite “people-space-activity” interaction framework. They further operationalized this construct for empirical analysis through three core quantitative metrics: activity density, activity duration, and activity diversity (Osunkoya and Partanen, 2024). With respect to the spatial scale of scholarly inquiry into urban public space vitality, extant research has established a well-validated multi-tiered analytical framework, spanning macro scales (e.g., entire municipalities and administrative districts) and meso scales (e.g., waterfront corridors, neighborhood blocks, and residential communities), a body of empirical work has characterized the spatial heterogeneity and evolutionary dynamics of public space vitality across these nested spatial scales (Chen et al., 2023; Chen and Huang, 2024; Collins et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Huang et al. 2025; Lopez-Muley et al., 2025). Despite these substantive advancements, the ﬁeld faces a pronounced structural imbalance: macro-scale inquiries are widely saturated, while investigations of micro-scale public spaces remain critically scarce, with three core research gaps delineated as follows: ﬁrst, imbalanced distribution of scholarly output, as global scholarly output has historically focused on macro- and meso-scale spatial units, including municipalities, administrative districts, waterfront corridors, and large urban plazas, with this body of work accounting for over 70% of all publications in the ﬁeld, while in contrast, dedicated investigations into micro-scale public spaces – including pocket parks, street-corner open spaces, and waterfront micro-nodes, which are most directly aligned with residents’ daily recreational needs and neighborhood-level social interaction – represent less than 10% of the total published literature (A et al., 2020). While international scholarship shifted its analytical focus from city-wide analyses to neighborhood-scale community life circles much earlier, bibliometric analysis of literature published between 2005 and 2024 reveals that dedicated studies of micro-scale public space vitality account for only 12% of the relevant scholarship, and furthermore, extant work in this domain is largely limited to descriptive analyses of planning and design practices for isolated case examples, with few studies undertaking systematic empirical interrogation of the core driving mechanisms underpinning vitality generation in these spaces (Wu and Chen, 2021; Doan and Zhang, 2025). Second, mismatch between mainstream analytical frameworks and micro-scale research contexts, as mainstream analytical frameworks for public space vitality are almost exclusively derived from empirical ﬁndings in macro- and meso-scale studies, rooted in the established analytical paradigm of “functional mix – development intensity – spatial vitality”, while by contrast, micro-scale public spaces exhibit unique, deﬁning characteristics: limited spatial footprint, relatively homogeneous functional typologies, and clearly deﬁned service catchments and targeted end-user groups, and the generation and evolutionary dynamics of spatial vitality in these spaces are governed by a distinctive generative mechanism, following the sequential pathway of “ﬁne-grained built environment optimization – scenario-based functional catalysis – full-cycle daily activity activation”, which means that established analytical frameworks are ill-suited to address the speciﬁc requirements of vitality research in these micro-scale contexts (Cheng and Li, 2025; Lyu et al., 2025). Third, inherent methodological limitations of prevailing analytical approaches for micro-scale inquiry, as with respect to methodological innovation, prevailing big data-driven analytical approaches have inherent limitations when applied to examine micro-scale public space vitality, speciﬁcally, GPS trajectory data, limited by ﬁxed temporal sampling intervals and coarse spatial resolution, cannot reliably capture ﬁne-grained user behavioral trajectories within these compact, spatially constrained settings, and compounding this challenge, emerging technologies including street view imagery and machine learning remain signiﬁcantly limited in their capacity to quantify the three-dimensional morphological attributes and ﬁne-grained activity dynamics of microscale spaces, a constraint that further restricts the depth of empirical inquiry into micro-scale public space vitality (Li et al., 2021; Oda and Yoshimura, 2024). Regarding the determinants driving spatial vitality outcomes, while extant research has systematically identiﬁed a well-validated suite of core attributes governing public space vitality, including spatial morphology, functional

First, scholarly inquiry into the spatial morphological drivers of vitality has long been predominantly limited to two-dimensional (2D) planar metrics, with remarkably little systematic investigation into the mechanisms through which threedimensional (3D) spatial morphological metrics shape vitality dynamics. Extant studies have overwhelmingly focused on 2D planar metrics such as site area and road network conﬁguration, quantifying their associations with spatial vitality (Shi et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022; Kafrawy et al., 2022; Lyu et al., 2025), yet have largely overlooked the fundamental mechanistic role of 3D spatial morphological attributes including spatial openness, height-to-width ratio, vertical interface permeability, and vertical facility layout (Ding and Wang, 2024; Lin et al., 2022). Second, the mechanistic linkage between on-site activity dynamics and public space vitality remains critically under-explored, with prior research failing to delineate the causal pathways through which activity-related attributes of public spaces shape vitality outcomes (Zhu et al., 2020). The majority of extant research has relied on the static functional mix index as the core explanatory variable to quantify its association with spatial vitality, while overlooking the independent and interactive effects of core activity attributes on vitality, including activity typologies, activity intensity, temporal dynamics, and user group suitability (Kim, 2020; Zeng et al., 2025). With respect to evidence-based public space vitality enhancement strategies, while extant research has extensively focused on optimizing vitality enhancement strategies and establishing systematic implementation frameworks for public spaces across nested spatial scales (Han et al., 2021; Dizdaroglu, 2022; Üzümcüoğlu and Polay, 2024; Chen et al., 2025), two knowledge gaps remain pervasive in the extant scholarly literature. First, a rigorous, context-speciﬁc methodological framework tailored to vitality analysis in micro-scale public spaces has yet to be systematically established. Traditional qualitative methodological approaches, including structured questionnaire surveys and systematic behavioral mapping, cannot robustly capture ﬁne-grained micro-level behavioral dynamics within compact, spatially bounded micro-scale settings. Meanwhile, prevailing quantitative analytical techniques, including space syntax and machine learning algorithms, have well-documented limitations in quantifying ﬁne-grained threedimensional (3D) spatial attributes and capturing time-varying activity dynamics within micro-scale contexts (Chen et al., 2019; Botta and Gutiérrez-Roig, 2021). Further compounding these methodological constraints, the integrated application of mixed-methods qualitative-quantitative approaches remains piecemeal, with no standardized analytical paradigm has been operationalized for this emerging ﬁeld of inquiry (Zhou et al., 2024). Second, existing vitality enhancement strategies are hindered by a fundamental misalignment between broad generalizability and targeted context-speciﬁc applicability. The majority of empirical studies in this domain are based on macro- and meso-scale case studies, with an overwhelming focus on generic intervention strategies, most commonly centered on improving transport connectivity and enhancing functional and commercial mix. In contrast, there remains a critical lack of systematic synthesis of context-responsive micro-renewal and precision placemaking interventions explicitly tailored to micro-scale public spaces. Furthermore, extant research has failed to adequately account for the functional heterogeneity of vitality generation mechanisms across public spaces with distinct primary functions, including ecological conservation, residential living, and commercial-business public spaces. Consequently, existing vitality enhancement frameworks deliver only limited actionable guidance and lack practical on-the-ground implementations for real-world urban planning practice (Cheng and Li, 2025). Waterfront public spaces constitute a foundational and irreplaceable component of the urban public space system, and people-centered, vitality-oriented placemaking for these spaces delivers multifaceted synergistic co-beneﬁts spanning ecological conservation, social interaction facilitation, and cultural heritage continuity (Bruns-Berentelg et al., 2022; Higazy, 2024; Zeng et al., 2025). The Hangzhou Section of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal (hereafter referred to as the Grand Canal waterfront), as a core waterfront segment of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, represents a strategically critical urban waterfront corridor in Hangzhou, embodying three core overlapping attributes: ecological carrying capacity, cultural heritage value, and public service functionality. Systematic enhancement of public space vitality along this corridor therefore holds profound exemplary value for advancing the

development of the Grand Canal National Cultural Park and informing the sustainable governance of World Heritage waterfront sites globally (Cai and Peng, 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). Over the past ﬁve years, following the full phased rollout and implementation of planning and construction initiatives for the Hangzhou section of the Grand Canal National Cultural Park, waterfront public spaces along the corridor have undergone a paradigm shift from singlepurpose landscape beautiﬁcation to integrated culture-tourism functional integration (Bian et al., 2024). Despite this transformative shift, these waterfront spaces still face persistent bottlenecks that constrain vitality enhancement, most notably inefﬁcient land utilization, widespread spatial enclosure and low interface permeability, and the limited spillover effect of organized functional activities. More speciﬁcally, micro-scale waterfront public spaces along the corridor are widely hindered by two core shortcomings: ill-considered built environment planning and design, and a critical mismatch between the supplied functional typologies and the differentiated needs of end-user groups. These shortcomings highlight an urgent need for evidence-based, targeted optimization interventions. To systematically address the multi-dimensional critical knowledge gaps identiﬁed in the systematic literature review, this study selects 56 micro-scale waterfront public spaces along the Hangzhou section of the Beijing- Hangzhou Grand Canal as the empirical research sample. Grounded in a systematic integration of foundational theories of urban public space vitality—including Jane Jacobs’s the Theory of Urban Diversity, Kevin Lynch’s Theory of the Image of the City, Jan Gehl’s Theory of Social Space, and Wayne Attoe and Donn Logan’s Urban Catalyst Theory—this study develops and operationalizes a multi-dimensional analytical indicator system anchored in the tripartite core analytical framework of “built environment (including three-dimensional spatial morphology) – functional activities – spatial vitality”. This study establishes two interlinked core research objectives: (1) To identify statistically signiﬁcant key characteristic elements driving the vitality of Grand Canal waterfront public spaces via correlation analysis; (2) To delineate the heterogeneous nonlinear relationships between key characteristic elements spatial vitality across three functional typologies of Grand Canal waterfront public spaces, namely ecological conservation, commercial-business, and residential living, and further quantify the response thresholds of key characteristic elements. This study makes three core contributions to advancing the scholarly understanding of urban public space vitality: (1) Theoretically, it ﬁlls the well-documented, longstanding critical research gap in micro-scale public space inquiry, and develops and empirically validates a context-speciﬁc tripartite analytical framework of “built environment – functional activities – spatial vitality”, tailored explicitly to micro-scale waterfront contexts, by systematically incorporating previously understudied multi-dimensional spatial attributes, most critically three-dimensional spatial morphology and ﬁne-grained functional activity dynamics. (2) Practically, it unpacks the causal effects of built environment and functional activity characteristic elements on spatial vitality along the Grand Canal waterfront, quantiﬁes the response thresholds of key characteristic elements that shape vitality outcomes, and formulates targeted, evidence-based placemaking strategies for Grand Canal waterfront public spaces ﬁrmly rooted in these empirically derived threshold values. This work directly addresses two pervasive, longstanding limitations of existing vitality enhancement frameworks: a systemic bias toward macro-scale generalizations at the expense of micro-scale context speciﬁcity, and a widespread overreliance on qualitative descriptive guidance rather than quantitative, empirically validated decision-support tools. (3) Methodologically, by integrating a complementary set of spatial econometric and geospatial analytical techniques – including multi-source geospatial data collection and preprocessing, Global Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation analysis, ArcGIS-based geospatial processing, correlation analysis, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)-related and Spatial Lag Model (SLM)-related regression– this study establishes a systematic, fourstage sequential optimization framework for vitality enhancement in the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces, comprising spatial pattern characterization of public space vitality, correlation analysis between characteristic elements and vitality, empirical identiﬁcation of response thresholds for key driving characteristic elements, and the development of targeted enhancement strategies. This analytical workﬂow provides a replicable methodological framework to support the quality improvement and performance enhancement of urban public spaces against the global backdrop of stock urban renewal.

## Research method

Study area

Hangzhou, the provincial capital of Zhejiang Province, is situated in the eastern coastal region of China, falling within the southern wing of the Yangtze River Delta and the Qiantang River Basin. Characterized by a humid subtropical monsoon climate with clear four seasons, the city records a long-term annual average temperature of 17.8 °C and an annual mean precipitation of 1454 mm. As of the end of 2024, Hangzhou has a year-end permanent resident population of 12.5 million, with a nominal gross domestic product (GDP) of CNY 2.1 trillion. Administratively and economically, it is ofﬁcially designated as a key regional central city on the southern wing of the Yangtze River Delta, as well as the national hub for digital economy innovation and high-quality development in China. The Hangzhou Section of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal – an ofﬁcially inscribed integral component of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Grand Canal – extends continuously from Tangqi Town in Yuhang District to the Sanbao Ship Lock on the Qiantang River, with a total main channel length of approximately 39 km. It traverses multiple heterogeneous urban functional zones within Hangzhou, including ecological conservation, commercialbusiness, and residential districts (Fig. 1). Throughout the millennial history of urban development in Hangzhou, which is characterized by the long-standing symbiotic relationship between the city and its water systems, this canal section – as one of the few remaining continuously navigable ancient canal segments worldwide – has capitalized on its unique locational endowments and status as a regional multimodal transport hub to evolve into a multi-functional core urban growth pole. It not only encapsulates the profound historical and cultural connotations of the Grand Canal system, but also serves as a core anchor for Hangzhou’s socioeconomic development. From a functional perspective, ofﬁcial statistics as of the end of 2024 show that the canal’s annual waterborne cargo throughput exceeds 80 million tons, and it remains a core backbone corridor underpinning the regional freight logistics system. In addition to its core shipping and logistics functions, a continuous linear public open space corridor network – integrating cultural heritage conservation, ecological landscape placemaking, and public service provision – has been systematically constructed along the waterfront. This network has become a strategic spatial framework for connecting Hangzhou’s key urban functional zones and improving the livability and quality of urban human settlements.

Sample selection and buffer zone deﬁnition

Sample selection

This study employs a methodological workﬂow for sample screening, spatial unit delineation, and buffer zone demarcation of micro-scale waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal, which is detailed in three sequential stages. First, representative micro-scale waterfront public spaces with diverse functional typologies along the canal – including historic blocks, cultural parks, pocket parks, community gardens, and waterfront micro-nodes – were

selected via systematic multi-criteria screening. The spatial boundaries of each sample unit were then rigorously delineated using clearly deﬁned natural and anthropogenic demarcation features, including urban arterial roads, green belts, and waterfront shorelines. Second, using the ﬁnalized validated vector boundaries of each delineated sample unit as input features, 500 m equidistant buffer zones were generated outward using the Euclidean Distance geoprocessing tool within ArcGIS 10.8. Finally, to resolve spatial overlaps between buffer zones of adjacent sample units, ﬁnal buffer boundary correction was conducted in strict accordance with a “Core Priority Allocation” principle. Speciﬁcally, under this standardized allocation framework, overlapping regions were assigned to the sample unit with the shortest Euclidean distance to its geometric centroid, in line with the supplementary “Nearest Centroid Allocation” decision rule. In cases of a tie, where the Euclidean distance from the centroids of two adjacent units to any given point in the overlapping region was equal, the overlapping area was objectively partitioned using the perpendicular bisector of the straight line connecting the midpoints of the original physical boundaries of the two adjacent units. By integrating systematic interpretation of high-resolution remote sensing imagery, multi-round systematic ﬁeld surveys, and iterative multi-source cross-validation, a ﬁnal sample of 56 waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal – each with representative site-speciﬁc attributes – was formally determined as the core empirical research sample units (Fig. 2). In strict accordance with the urban functional zoning criteria stipulated in the Hangzhou Territorial Spatial Master Plan (2021–2035) (Hangzhou Municipal People’s Government, 2025), the sample units were further classiﬁed into three functional typologies: ecological conservation, commercial-business, and residential living public spaces. This standardized classiﬁcation framework provides an analytical basis for the subsequent typology-speciﬁc analysis of spatial vitality dynamics and their underlying driving mechanisms across the Grand Canal waterfront study area.

Deﬁnition of the 500 m buffer zone

In this study, the delineation of the 500 m buffer zone for waterfront public spaces adjacent to the Grand Canal was aligned with the regulatory speciﬁcations set out in the Urban Design Guidelines for Territorial Spatial Planning (2021 Draft for Approval, hereafter referred to as the Guidelines) issued by the Ministry of Natural Resources of China (MNR, 2021). The Guidelines explicitly deﬁne that 500 m is the standard walking catchment radius of urban public spaces to serve residents’ daily recreational use, a threshold that constitutes the core spatial unit for guaranteeing the accessibility of public services within the 15-min community life circle. Meanwhile, from an international perspective, a buffer interval of 400–800 m (equivalent to a 5–15-min walking duration) for evaluating public space accessibility is widely embedded in both the global guidelines for sustainable urban development issued by the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) and urban planning practices in developed countries across Europe and North America (Citaristi, 2022). To further verify the applicability of the 500 m buffer zone conﬁguration adopted in this study, we established three comparative buffer zone scenarios (300 m, 500 m, and 800 m). We conducted a comparative validation analysis using two core evaluation metrics: the explanatory power of model ﬁtting (R² value) and model goodness-of-ﬁt (Akaike Information Criterion [AIC] value) of spatial econometric models developed for each buffer zone scenario (Table 1). The coefﬁcient of determination (R²) quantiﬁes the explanatory power of the spatial models built with each corresponding buffer zone for the target variables, with values closer to 1.0 indicating stronger model explanatory performance. The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) evaluates the goodness-of-ﬁt of the regression models developed for each corresponding buffer zone, with smaller values indicating more robust and reliable model ﬁtting performance. Validation results for the three comparative buffer schemes consistently demonstrate that the 500 m buffer scheme attains the highest R² and the lowest AIC, and outperforms the remaining two alternative schemes overall. This dual performance advantage corroborates that the delineation of the 500 m buffer zone not only is fully consistent with the standard walking catchment radius for residents’ daily recreational use, but also guarantees superior goodness of ﬁt and statistical robustness for the subsequent spatial modeling. On this basis, the 500 m buffer scheme is formally selected as the most theoretically consistent, empirically robust, and methodologically appropriate spatial analysis unit for the empirical analysis in this study.

Research framework

This study develops an analytical research framework, consisting of several core modules (Fig. 3).

Theoretical integration and indicator system construction

Rooted in classical urban planning and human settlement theory, we systematically synthesized four foundational theoretical frameworks: Jane Jacobs’s Theory of Urban Diversity, Kevin Lynch’s Theory of the Image of the City, Jan Gehl’s Theory of Social Space, and Wayne Attoe and Donn Logan’s Urban Catalyst Theory. Anchored in the widely validated “built environment – functional activities – spatial vitality” analytical paradigm, we developed and implemented a rigorous three-stage indicator screening and validation protocol: initial indicator construction via theoretical deduction, secondary indicator puriﬁcation using the Delphi method, and ﬁnal indicator determination via the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Following this, we established and ﬁnalized a hierarchical indicator system consisting of 3 primary indicators, 13 secondary indicators, and 44 tertiary indicators, which forms a multidimensional indicator framework for the spatial vitality of waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal. This framework possesses ﬁve core advantages: scientiﬁc rigor, structural systematicity, quantitative measurability, data accessibility, and context-speciﬁc applicability tailored to the Grand Canal waterfront study area.

Identiﬁcation of key driving characteristic elements

First, we performed the Shapiro-Wilk test to verify the normal distribution characteristics of the preprocessed multisource spatiotemporal dataset for all indicators. Subsequently, based on the results of the normality test, we selected a correlation analysis approach tailored to the data distribution characteristics, to systematically examine the multivariate associations between built environment characteristic elements, functional activity characteristic elements, and the spatial vitality of the Grand Canal waterfront public space sample units. Finally, on this basis, we empirically identiﬁed the key built environment and functional activity characteristic elements that exert a statistically signiﬁcant dominant effect on the spatial vitality of urban waterfront public spaces.

Multi-source data acquisition and standardized preprocessing for indicators

For the three core dimensions of our theoretically grounded indicator system, we detail the standardized workﬂows for the acquisition, cleaning, calibration, and preprocessing of multi-source spatiotemporal data.

Spatial vitality data

We collected continuous, full-coverage pedestrian ﬂow data for the 56 sampled waterfront public spaces across 91 consecutive days from September to November 2024, using anonymized mobile phone signaling records and Wi-Fi probe sensing systems. We subsequently extracted three core vitality indicators from this dataset: average daily active population, average per capita dwell time, and intra-week volatility coefﬁcient. To enable methodological triangulation and robust cross-validation of the mobile phone signaling dataset, we additionally collected social interaction density data using a time-stratiﬁed ﬁxed-point behavioral observation protocol (4 independent observation sessions were conducted on both weekdays and statutory public holidays, with a minimum cumulative observation duration of 12 hours for each sampled study unit).

Physical environment data

All physical environment indicators were quantiﬁed via multi-source geospatial big data fusion techniques, with detailed data sources and standardized processing workﬂows elaborated as follows: High-resolution remote sensing imagery, building footprint vector data, and land use status survey data were adopted to derive indicators characterizing land use composition and landscape environmental attributes. OpenStreetMap (OSM) vector data and Baidu Point of Interest (POI) datasets were employed to generate indicators quantifying road network topological characteristics and the spatial distribution of public service facilities. Equidistantly sampled panoramic street view imagery (with a minimum of 5 sampling points set for each study unit, covering all primary pedestrian corridors and core activity nodes within the target waterfront public spaces) was processed via a pre-trained semantic segmentation model to extract three-dimensional morphological indicators, including Sky View Factor, Height-to-Width Ratio, etc., which characterize the spatial openness of the study sites. Supplementary indicators, including locational centrality and public transport station accessibility, were calculated using the Network Analyst module embedded in ArcGIS 10.8.

In addition, our results further corroborate the tenets of urban vitality theory: that accessibility constitutes the foundational prerequisite for the generation of outdoor activities, while the adequate provision of public service facilities serves as the critical underpinning for sustained user retention and activity participation. We further reveal that these factors jointly form a “window of opportunity” for residents’ recreational behaviors, which serve as the core preconditions that shape users’ decision-making regarding visits to public spaces and participation in on-site recreational activities. Conversely, our study reveals that indicators of land use – including ﬂoor area ratio, building density, and land use mix degree – as well as indicators of spatial openness – including vacant land ratio, height-to-width ratio, and building setback distance, exert no statistically signiﬁcant effects on the vitality of the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces, and even exhibit marginally signiﬁcant negative correlations under speciﬁc contextual conditions. This ﬁnding is notably inconsistent with prior empirical conclusions derived from “land use-driven” urban vitality frameworks (Zeng et al. 2018; Üzümcüoğlu and Polay, 2024). We argue that, in macro-scale analyses that take administrative districts or sub-districts as the analytical unit, a higher ﬂoor area ratio and greater land use mix typically indicate stronger population agglomeration potential and more intensive economic activity, which can generate sufﬁcient visitor ﬂow to support spatial vitality, and are thus identiﬁed as core drivers for enhancing the vitality of urban public spaces. However, when the analytical unit is downscaled to the micro-scale of public spaces, the generative mechanisms of spatial vitality undergo a fundamental paradigm shift: spatial vitality is no longer solely dependent on visitor ﬂow spillovers from surrounding areas, but is predominantly driven by the site’s intrinsic environmental quality, activity carrying capacity, and functional scenario adaptability. For the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces investigated in this study, high-intensity land development in the surrounding areas consistently erodes the recreational attractiveness of these waterfront sites through multiple pathways, including closed spatial interfaces, excessive visual enclosure, and ambient noise interference, which signiﬁcantly constrains their capacity to support sustained user retention and on-site activity participation (Table 5). On this basis, the unilateral improvement of land use intensity and land use mix cannot be automatically converted into spatial vitality enhancement for the micro-scale individual waterfront public space units examined in this study. The non-signiﬁcant correlation between spatial openness indicators and spatial vitality can be systematically explained via the theoretical framework of multi-functional attributes and inherent trade-off mechanisms in waterfront complex systems. Prior studies focusing on single-functional public spaces, including urban plazas and neighborhood parks, have consistently veriﬁed that improved spatial openness can effectively expand activity carrying capacity, enhance the visual quality of the built environment, and thus promote the vitality of urban public spaces. However, the Grand Canal waterfront system examined in this study is a complex multi-functional nexus integrating ﬂood control and water conservancy, inland waterway navigation, cultural heritage conservation, ecological protection, and recreational use, with inherent multi-dimensional trade-offs between competing functional objectives (Ragheb et al., 2024). This attribute forms signiﬁcant practical constraints on the recreation-oriented demand for improved spatial openness. Speciﬁcally, to guarantee the delivery of core non-recreational functions including inland navigation and ﬂood control, waterfront spaces with high vacant land ratios and sky view factor are often preferentially zoned for waterway operational uses, including port terminals, freight storage yards, and ship berths. Although these spaces have high nominal spatial openness, their operational function not only encroaches on the available recreational space, but also breaks the physical and visual continuity of the waterfront interface. This leads to a fundamental mismatch with the core design requirements of recreational public spaces – accessibility, user comfort, and safety – which ultimately explains the absence of a statistically signiﬁcant positive correlation between spatial openness indicators and spatial vitality (Table 6). Drawing on the full set of ﬁndings and theoretical insights elaborated above, we propose the following targeted, evidence-based optimization strategies to enhance the vitality of the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces via physical environment improvement: (1) Prioritize the targeted improvement of public transport station accessibility, water surface ratio, and cultural and sports public service facility density within the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces and their surrounding buffer zones. In parallel, improve the supply of supporting infrastructure and service systems to support the organization of diverse, high-quality recreational activities.

Optimization strategies for Grand Canal waterfront public space vitality from functional activity dimension

Functional diversity and activity multiplicity are the foundational tenets of vitality in urban public spaces, and form the indispensable mediating mechanism that underpins the transformation of the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces from passive spatial carriers to active vitality-generating places. Our ﬁndings consistently veriﬁed that functional integration degree and the economic value generated by functional activities exert statistically signiﬁcant positive driving effects on the vitality of waterfront public spaces. This ﬁnding indicates that the richness, complementarity, and economic value creation capacity of activity types within public spaces are the primary drivers of visitor agglomeration, prolonged average per capita dwell time, and improved utilization intensity of public spaces. Meanwhile, indicators related to the inﬂuence of functional activities – including public attention, public usage degree, and media attention – exhibit marginally signiﬁcant yet stable positive correlations with public space vitality. This ﬁnding is highly consistent with prior empirical evidence from Mouratidis and Poortinga (2020) and Guo et al. (2022), which revealed the reciprocal interaction mechanism between vitality perception and social feedback in urban public spaces. This ﬁnding further veriﬁes that, while the inﬂuence scale of functional activities is not a core driver of spatial vitality, it acts as a key catalyst for the spatial diffusion and scale expansion of public space vitality. A particularly counterintuitive ﬁnding emerging from our empirical analysis is that the environmental value generated by functional activities exerts a statistically signiﬁcant negative effect on the vitality of waterfront public spaces. This ﬁnding directly addresses and advances the long-standing international academic debate on the trade-offs and synergies between the multi-functional attributes of waterfront complex systems: existing international scholarship has formed two competing theoretical perspectives on the relationship between ecological protection and vitality enhancement in waterfront public spaces (Avni and Teschner, 2019; Liu et al., 2026). The ﬁrst perspective, grounded in ecosystem service theory, argues that improving the ecological quality of waterfront public spaces can enhance the value of landscape amenities, thus realizing the synergistic improvement of ecological protection and spatial vitality. The second perspective, rooted in conservation governance theory for ecologically sensitive areas, holds that the stringent regulatory requirements of ecological protection will compress the spatial scope of recreational activities and limit the type and scale of recreational events, leading to an inherent trade-off between the two objectives. This conﬂict is particularly prominent in the Grand Canal waterfront system, which undertakes core functions including ecological protection, inland waterway navigation, and cultural heritage conservation. Our ﬁndings provide evidence to support the second theoretical perspective. For linear riparian corridor systems represented by the Grand Canal, which are characterized by high ecological sensitivity and strict heritage conservation regulatory constraints, high-participation public recreational events (e.g., marathons and large-scale cultural festivals) will inevitably cause adverse ecological disturbances, including vegetation trampling, aquatic ecosystem damage, solid waste generation, and anthropogenic noise pollution. On the contrary, the regulatory measures implemented by local administrative authorities to fulﬁll mandatory ecological protection requirements – including visitor volume caps, event approval restrictions, and temporary spatial closures— directly reduce the public’ s willingness to participate in on-site recreational activities. This interaction forms a self-reinforcing negative feedback loop of “ecological protection regulation—restricted recreational behavior — declining spatial vitality”, which clearly reveals the causal mechanism behind the signiﬁcant negative correlation between environmental value and public space vitality observed in this study.

Scenario simulation and prediction of vitality based on temperature variation

Situated in the subtropical monsoon climate zone, Hangzhou is characterized by signiﬁcant seasonal heterogeneity in ambient temperature. Extreme low temperatures in winter and extreme high temperatures in summer exert a pronounced restrictive effect on outdoor recreational activities in waterfront spaces. The analysis in this study is solely based on in-situ measured spatial vitality data collected from September to November 2024 (the autumn season in Hangzhou), and thus fails to elucidate the driving mechanisms of spatial vitality under different temperature regimes across spring, summer, and winter. ## Conclusions

Taking 56 waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal as the research sample units, this study addresses the welldocumented critical research gap characterized by the saturation of macro-scale studies and a notable lack of microscale empirical analyses in the existing international scholarship on urban public space vitality. Grounded in four foundational theories from classical urban planning scholarship – including Jane Jacobs’ Theory of Urban Diversity, Kevin Lynch’s Theory of the Image of City, Jan Gehl’s Theory of Social Space, and Wayne Attoe and Donn Logan’s Urban Catalyst Theory – we constructed and operationalized a multi-dimensional analytical framework and corresponding indicator system anchored in the tripartite analytical nexus of “built environment (including threedimensional spatial morphology) – functional activities – spatial vitality”. Via correlation analysis and multi-model nonlinear ﬁtting, we identiﬁed the statistically signiﬁcant key characteristic elements that shape the vitality of waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal, delineated the heterogeneous nonlinear relationships between these core determinants and spatial vitality across ecological conservation, commercial-business, and residential living public spaces, and quantitatively identiﬁed the response thresholds of core determinants required to achieve the prespeciﬁed Grade I spatial vitality targets deﬁned in the Urban Design Guidelines for Territorial Spatial Planning. This study provides an empirically grounded scientiﬁc basis for evidence-based planning, design optimization, and functional layout adjustment of waterfront public spaces, while offering a replicable, scalable analytical framework for research on urban public space vitality. The key ﬁndings of this study are systematically summarized as follows: (1) The vitality of waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal exhibits statistically signiﬁcant temporal heterogeneity, with signiﬁcantly higher vitality levels recorded on weekends versus weekdays. This temporal differentiation pattern is stably and consistently reﬂected across multiple core vitality measurement indicators, including average daily active population, social interaction density, and average per capita dwell time. (2) Location centrality, public transport station accessibility, water surface ratio, cultural and sports public service facility density, and functional integration are identiﬁed as the statistically signiﬁcant core driving characteristic elements of waterfront public space vitality along the Grand Canal, and thus constitute the core regulatory levers for targeted vitality enhancement in subsequent planning and design practices. This core ﬁnding directly challenges the widespread overreliance of existing international scholarship and prevailing planning and construction strategies on land use intensity and two-dimensional planar spatial form as the dominant drivers of urban public space vitality enhancement. (3) By integrating the Spatial Lag Model (SLM) for spatial spillover effect correction, we corrected the raw in-situ measured spatial vitality values and quantitatively identiﬁed the critical response thresholds of the core spatial driving determinants required for commercial-business, residential living, and ecological conservation public space to meet the Grade I public space vitality standards stipulated in the Urban Design Guidelines for Territorial Spatial Planning. This empirical advance addresses the longstanding key limitation of existing urban public space vitality scholarship, which has long been dominated by qualitative interpretation and descriptive analysis, and advances the methodological transition from qualitative descriptive analysis to quantitative, empirically validated threshold measurement in the ﬁeld. This study contributes to the understudied micro-scale domain of urban public space vitality research, with its academic contributions centered on three dimensions: (1) Analytical framework development: We constructed and

(2) Methodological approach optimization: By integrating a complementary suite of technical and analytical methods including multi-source geospatial data acquisition and standardized preprocessing, Global Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation test, ArcGIS-based geospatial analysis, correlation analysis, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method, Spatial Lag Model (SLM)-corrected method, and regression analysis, we developed a standardized and replicable vitality enhancement pathway for waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal. This pathway follows a standardized, sequentially progressive workﬂow: “quantitative characterization of public space vitality – correlation analysis between key driving characteristic elements and spatial vitality– identiﬁcation of response thresholds for core driving characteristic elements – formulation of targeted, evidence-based optimization strategies”. By integrating the Global Moran’s I test and SLM correction framework, we effectively eliminated systematic estimation biases in correlation and regression analyses that arise from unaccounted spatial spillover effects of waterfront spatial vitality. (3) Empirical application value: We empirically focused on the core waterfront reach of the Hangzhou Section of Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal – a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site with integrated ecological conservation functions, irreplaceable cultural heritage value, and core urban public service attributes – as the empirical research context. For waterfront public spaces along the Grand Canal, we proposed evidence-based, threshold-informed planning and design optimization strategies, which directly address the two core limitations of prevailing planning strategies: speciﬁcally, the longstanding overreliance on macro-scale strategic analysis with limited micro-scale implementable guidance, and the dominance of qualitative descriptive recommendations over quantitative, operable threshold-based guidance. This study delineates the boundary conditions of three widely cited prevailing conclusions in extant international urban public space vitality research, including “high land use mix and high development intensity inevitably generate high spatial vitality”, “spatial openness has a signiﬁcant positive linear correlation with public space vitality”, and “ecological conservation and spatial vitality enhancement are inherently contradictory”. We empirically refute the universal applicability of these conclusions within the micro-scale waterfront public space context of this study, and identify the core pathway for vitality enhancement of the Grand Canal waterfront public spaces: “built environment optimization – scenario-based functional catalysis”. This work complements the established theoretical and analytical system of urban public space vitality research by constructing a complete, logically closed analytical loop spanning from linear correlation analysis to nonlinear threshold response quantiﬁcation. Furthermore, we developed two quantitative response functions: “temperature – spatial vitality” and “regional economic development level – spatial vitality”, to enhance the external generalizability of our research ﬁndings and establish a standardized quantitative framework for spatial vitality prediction across full seasonal cycles and heterogeneous urban economic development contexts. A key limitation of this study lies in the fact that we did not conduct further multi-context validation of the external generalizability of the constructed “key characteristic elements – spatial vitality” nonlinear regression curves and response thresholds across heterogeneous geographic contexts and waterfront space typologies. Future research should expand the analytical scope to cover waterfront public spaces across diverse geographic regions, functional typologies and development contexts, and explicitly delineate the boundary conditions for the transferability of the technical analytical framework and core ﬁndings of this study to heterogeneous waterfront contexts, to ultimately construct a larger multi-scenario sample dataset and derive more systematic and widely generalizable research conclusions.
